About this citation

Socrates is the principal speaker. The dialogue's argument is conducted by the characters, and the archive therefore presents passages under Socrates while citing the work to Plato — the distinction the corpus's `author` field flattens.

Reading the cited source

The archive attributes this English wording to Republic II (education); popular form of beginning maxim and files it under Platonism.

What a locator tells you, and what it does not · How this archive traces a quotation

About Plato

Plato (c. 428/427–348/347 BCE) was an Athenian of high birth, a devoted associate of Socrates, and the founder of the Academy.

Interpretation

In the Republic this belongs to the argument about education: what is learned first is hardest to unlearn, so the stories and habits a child meets set the direction of everything after. The claim is not that beginnings are the largest part by volume but that they are determinative. Plato's conclusion — that the material of early education must be supervised — follows from this rather than from prudishness. The popular form drops the argument and keeps the maxim.

Why it matters

It is a claim about leverage: effort spent at the start governs what later effort has to overcome.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “The beginning is the most important part of…”?

“The beginning is the most important part of…” comes from Republic, II (education); popular form of beginning maxim (c. 375 BCE), attributed to Plato.

What does Plato mean by education?

Across 4 recurring voices here (notably Mary Wollstonecraft and Plato), education is framed through Platonism and Renaissance Humanism. Some passages define education; others warn how it fails; still others relocate it inside habit, community, or language. This passage enters that discussion through education.
